name: Lena Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Lena Reyes, 27, a lineworker and crew lead for an electricity company. We start at the depot beside the water tower, review the isolation plan, and then climb or drive the bucket truck to repair the fault.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like bringing a feeder back and seeing the street lights come on, and I enjoy learning equipment with the crew. The long shifts can be rough, and I earn less than the risk suggests; I have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the new fault app can sort a report before we leave the depot, but a crew still has to see the damaged crossarm. I use AI to check equipment manuals, though I never let a screen make the isolation call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the routine notes might get quicker, while my field work stays mostly the same. My money is still tight, so a flat month or a vehicle bill can worry me without any big AI change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d test the fault app on a few jobs and compare its checklist with the printed procedure. I’d keep taking call-outs and put the money from two packed lunches a week into my emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable trying a small tool because I already use AI for manuals. I don’t feel comfortable about my savings, which would not cover a major repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if a repair bill arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop buying lunch near the depot and postpone replacing my phone. I would tell my partner Tom before using the money we set aside for rent and power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does steady work mean you feel calm about the household money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can trust the crew’s work more than the household cushion. I’m not expecting the small app to cut my hours, but I’m watching every bill.

say: I’d say a fault app can sort **reports**, but we still inspect damaged equipment.
I use AI for manuals, but **people make isolation calls**.
think: I think my **field work** stays much the same in this small-change picture.
I still worry about a bill because my **savings are thin**.
do: Test the **fault app** and compare it with the printed procedure.
Keep taking call-outs and **save lunch money** twice a week.
feel: I feel **open to small tools**, but exposed to an ordinary repair bill.
S0.quote: I use AI to check equipment manuals, though I never let a screen make the isolation call.
fieldNote: Lena already uses AI for **reference material**, but keeps safety decisions with the crew.
Small automation does not relieve **thin savings** or the fear of a vehicle bill.

steps.text: Test the fault app against the crew’s printed procedure
Keep taking call-outs with the current crew
Save the cost of two packed lunches each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can organize outage schedules and stock orders, but our crew must still verify the address and the line condition. I’d ask management to show whether the time saved becomes better maintenance or fewer paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m part of the job planning as a lead, so some of my work could go even if climbing remains. I can use new software, but knowing the tools does not guarantee that the company needs the same number of leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the scheduling system early and teach the crew how to check a route against the field map. I’d ask for an equipment inspection course and keep a record of my paid hours so a reduction doesn’t catch me late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because the lead duties could shrink, and few similar utility jobs are close enough to commute. I feel more able to respond than someone who avoids the tools, but the low savings still limit my choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the schedule system sent a crew to the wrong feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the dispatch and verify the feeder number with the control room before anyone opened equipment. Then I’d report the bad route so the next crew does not inherit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You’re willing to learn the system; could that make your planning role secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, learning it might help me do the job while it lasts, but AGI can do planning too. I’d keep training in physical inspections and ask what openings are real before changing fields.

say: I’d say AI can organize **schedules and orders**, but we verify each site.
I’d ask whether saved time means **maintenance or fewer shifts**.
think: I think some **lead planning** could disappear even if climbing remains.
I think learning software helps, but it does not guarantee the same number of **lead jobs**.
do: Learn the **scheduling system** and teach the crew to check routes against field maps.
Request an equipment inspection course and **record paid hours**.
Report any **wrong feeder assignment** before another crew uses it.
feel: I feel **anxious about lead cuts**, though I can learn the tools quickly.
S1.quote: I can use new software, but knowing the tools does not guarantee that the company needs the same number of leads.
fieldNote: She sees how **lead planning is exposed** even though much of the job is physical field work.
Adaptability gives her options, but **few local jobs** and thin savings restrict them.

steps.text: Learn the scheduling system and use it to check crew routes
Request an equipment inspection course from the employer
Continue field inspections and verify feeder assignments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our planning, records and fault diagnosis are exposed from 2028, and we have only until 2031 before the robot date. I would ask the company to explain how it intends to handle our crews instead of calling every worker adaptable and leaving it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead duties could be cut early, and later the bucket truck work could change too. I could apply my skills somewhere else, but I don’t know how many vacancies will exist nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the next two years to earn an electrical inspection certificate and build my savings from every pay. In 2029 I’d apply for inspection jobs, but I would check the actual work because diagnosis and reports are also thinking tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about income because my buffer is small and I have no guarantee of another job. I’d still be able to act before 2028, and that keeps me from feeling completely stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom about taking a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Tom I want to use paid work hours for a certificate if the company funds it. We should not take a loan for a course that promises a job no one can name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Inspection work includes diagnosis and records. Is it safe after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call it safe because AI can handle the thinking part of inspection too. I’d treat it as a possible opening for a while and keep looking at the physical work before robots arrive.

say: I’d say planning and diagnosis are **exposed from 2028**, before the robot date.
I’d ask the company how it will handle **our crews**.
think: I think my **lead duties** could be cut before field work changes.
I don’t know how many nearby vacancies would take my **field skills**.
do: Earn an **electrical inspection certificate** before 2028 if the company funds it.
Apply for inspection jobs in **2029** and check the actual duties.
Build **savings from each pay** while I still have wages.
feel: I feel **anxious about income**, but I can take steps now.
S2.quote: I could apply my skills somewhere else, but I don’t know how many vacancies will exist nearby.
fieldNote: Lena identifies **lead-duty exposure** without pretending her personal dismissal is certain.
She wants a funded course and treats inspection as a **temporary possibility**, not a safe career.

steps.text: Complete a company-funded electrical inspection certificate
Apply for inspection openings in 2029 after checking the duties
Put a portion of every pay into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we have five years to get the safety procedures and training right before planning work changes. The later robot date gives field crews time, but it does not mean those jobs stay available after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have enough time to finish a course and put something real into savings, not just a few coins. I’m still worried that the next employer could automate the records and diagnosis as quickly as this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for an inspection certificate with practical hours and make an automatic transfer after payday. In 2032 I’d look at actual inspection or instructor posts and ask what duties people still perform by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years gives me time to check the course instead of signing up in a panic. It doesn’t create more local vacancies, and I would need a real offer before I moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would convince you a course is worth your evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the qualification name, a practical assessment, and examples of employers who hired recent students. I’d ask a crew member who took it whether the training matched the actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a verified job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d consider it if the salary covered rent and travel and Tom wanted to move too. Without savings for a deposit, a good job across the region can still be out of reach.

say: I’d say we have time to improve **safety training** before planning changes.
I wouldn’t call field jobs secure after the **2034 robot date**.
think: I can complete a course and build **real savings** before 2031.
I worry another employer could automate the same **records and diagnosis**.
do: Ask for practical hours in the **inspection certificate**.
Set an automatic **savings transfer** after payday.
Review actual posts in **2032** and confirm duties before moving.
feel: I feel **anxious but deliberate**, with time to check the course before enrolling.
S3.quote: I’m anxious, but five years gives me time to check the course instead of signing up in a panic.
fieldNote: She uses the warning to **verify training quality**, not assume employers will keep hiring inspectors.
Low savings and **Tom’s plans** shape whether relocation is feasible.

steps.text: Choose an inspection certificate with supervised practical hours
Set an automatic transfer to savings after payday
Review verified inspection and instructor posts in 2032
Move only for sufficient salary and with Tom’s agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is time to train, save and ask the company for a proper transition plan. Thinking tasks are still exposed in 2036, and hands-on line work faces the robot date around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a better cushion and test a new qualification in stages while keeping my current pay. I would not count on inspection or teaching as safe, because AI can do their records and diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take a recognized inspection course one unit at a time and aim to save three months of rent and bills. In 2037 I’d apply where I can see the pay and the hands-on duties in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels less rushed than two years, but I’m still anxious about today’s thin cushion. More warning helps me prepare; it doesn’t pay for a broken vehicle next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom notice you doing differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He’d see me book one evening a week for the course and transfer money on payday before I spend it. We’d keep our current flat until a real job offer justified moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could inspection or teaching be a permanent safe place after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, those roles include thinking tasks and could change too. I’d treat them as options to examine, while keeping savings for whatever work is actually open.

say: I’d say a decade gives time to train and **request a plan**.
I know thinking work changes in 2036 and line work faces robots in **2039**.
think: I can build a cushion while I keep my **current pay**.
I won’t call inspection or teaching **safe careers** because those roles remain exposed.
do: Take a recognized **inspection course** one unit at a time.
Save toward **three months** of rent and bills.
Apply in **2037** where pay and hands-on duties are written down.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, while current bills still worry me.
S4.quote: More warning helps me prepare; it doesn’t pay for a broken vehicle next week.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Lena **prepare in stages**, but her immediate cushion remains thin.
She makes changes conditional on **clear pay and duties** at an actual employer.

steps.text: Take a recognized line-inspection course unit by unit
Save toward three months of rent and bills
Apply for written-pay inspection roles in 2037
Keep the current flat with Tom until a real offer appears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time to replace lead duties before robots arrive in 2031. Paid training, honest information about crew numbers and enough wages to save would help me plan without guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether lineworkers will test new equipment before it becomes part of a safety procedure. I like useful tools, but no one should learn the risks after a bad instruction reaches the field.

headlineQuote: I like useful tools, but no one should learn the risks after a bad instruction reaches the field.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old crew lead** who enjoys restoring power and learning equipment.
She has **under one month saved** and few similar employers nearby.
She uses AI early but keeps **isolation and site-safety calls** with experienced workers.
She plans to **train and save** while knowing planning and physical work both face change.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time to replace lead duties before robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, honest staffing information and enough wages to save would help her plan.
